name: Hot-cold empathy gap
statement: People in a calm state underestimate how much hunger, pain, craving or arousal will change what they and other people want and do.
meaning: The idea comes from George Loewenstein's account of visceral factors: hunger, thirst, pain, fatigue, craving, fear and sexual arousal. His claim is that these states do two things at once. They shift what a person wants, and they are almost impossible to simulate from outside. A person who is not hungry cannot summon hunger the way she can summon a tune or a face, so her forecast of her hungry self is built on a theory rather than on a feeling. Three separate claims travel under the one name. The first is that visceral states change judgement, which is the easiest to test. The second is that a calm person underestimates that change in their own future self, the cold-to-hot gap. The third is that the same failure applies to other people, so a calm observer misjudges an aroused, craving or frightened one. Loewenstein's framework adds the reverse direction: a person in a hot state overestimates how long the state will last, and projects it onto others who are not in it. The three claims need different experiments, and the literature has tested them to very different depths.

origin.where: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
origin.note: The paper is a theoretical review with no new data. It lays out seven numbered propositions about visceral factors, of which proposition 5 is that people underestimate the impact of visceral factors on their own future behaviour and proposition 7 extends the first six to other people. The phrase 'hot-cold empathy gap' does not appear in it; the word Loewenstein uses is an 'empathic gulf', borrowed from Elaine Scarry on pain and widened from pain to hunger, fear and the rest. He titled a 2005 Health Psychology article 'Hot-cold empathy gaps and medical decision making'.

evidence: The most cited demonstration is Ariely and Loewenstein's arousal study. Thirty-five male Berkeley undergraduates were recruited by campus advertisements, paid $10 a session, and given a laptop to use at home. In the arousal sessions they masturbated and could answer questions only once they moved a slider past 75 on a self-reported arousal scale. Answers ran from 0 to 100. Eleven men did a non-aroused session only and drop out of the main comparison, which therefore rests on 24 men, t(23) throughout. Of 20 questions on the appeal of sexual activities, 16 shifted upward with arousal: anal sex from 46 to 77, tying up a partner from 47 to 75, attraction to a 12-year-old girl from 23 to 46, arousal by contact with an animal from 6 to 16. All five questions about procuring sex shifted: slipping a woman a drug from 5 to 26, continuing after a date says no from 20 to 45. Of eight questions on unsafe sex, the four that name a condom shifted and the other four did not. Sayette, Loewenstein, Griffin and Black ran the only test here in which a prediction is scored against the same person's later valuation. Ninety-eight smokers, mean age 27.1 and 17.2 cigarettes a day, were assigned to a hot condition, a cold condition or a comparison group that attended one session. In session one the hot group had abstained 12 hours and held a lit cigarette while the cold group had smoked normally and held a roll of tape. Urge ratings were 75.9 against 26.7, F(1, 73) = 61.03, p < .0001. Each man or woman named the smallest sum they would accept to delay smoking five minutes in session two a week later, then revised it in session two while craving. The cold group moved from $8.18 to $9.33, p < .05. The hot group moved from $9.53 to $8.77, not significant. The interaction is F(1, 72) = 7.83, p < .007. Van Boven and Loewenstein tested the version about other people. Their first study showed 39 students three hikers whose food a bear had eaten, in country the scenario says holds plenty of water. Most reported mentally trading places with them, 79% in open description and 87% when asked directly. A second study put 47 people before or after exercise on a stationary bicycle, a rowing machine or a stepping machine, and gave them different hikers, lost with no food and no water. Those who had just exercised were thirstier, 6.88 against 3.65, and more likely to say both they and the hikers would be more bothered by thirst than by hunger, all four comparisons at p < .05 or better.

examples.tag: The shopping list written after lunch
examples.text: A full shopper plans a week of modest meals and buys to the list. Hungry on Thursday evening he wants none of it, because the list was drawn up by someone who could not feel hunger at the time.

examples.tag: The friend who says just stop
examples.text: A non-smoker tells a smoker that the craving is only a habit. He is not withholding sympathy; he cannot summon the state he is being asked to picture, so he judges it from a theory of it instead.

examples.tag: The appointment booked while the pain has passed
examples.text: A patient whose back has stopped hurting cancels the physiotherapy he arranged during the worst week. Free of pain he cannot recover the state that made the booking seem necessary, and he reads his earlier self as having overreacted.

replication.headline: Two German-language studies by authors with no tie to Loewenstein reproduced the arousal effect in men and found it in women, with 84 and 86 participants, though the second holds only after 19 of the 86 are dropped.
replication.detail: Imhoff and Schmidt aroused men and women with recorded erotic narratives rather than masturbation and asked for self-estimated likelihood of sexual and non-sexual disinhibited behaviour. Study 1 recruited 84 students, Study 2 recruited 86. In Study 1 arousal raised sexual disinhibition, F(1, 66) = 9.16, p = .004, partial eta squared .12, with d = 0.94 in men and 0.51 in women, and left non-sexual disinhibition alone. Study 2 gave F(1, 63) = 5.55, p = .02, partial eta squared .086, with d = 0.48 in men and 0.67 in women. Both studies excluded people whose arousal ratings contradicted their condition, 16 in Study 1 and 19 in Study 2. Keeping them in leaves Study 1 significant, F(1, 82) = 3.98, p < .05, and leaves Study 2 short of it, F(1, 82) = 2.59, p = .11. What replicated is that responses move with the state. Neither study asked anyone to predict a future self or another person. Every figure here is read off the accepted manuscript, since no copy of the published article could be opened.

study.cite: Imhoff, R., & Schmidt, A. F. (2014). Sexual disinhibition under sexual arousal: Evidence for domain specificity in men and women. Archives of Sexual Behavior, 43(6), 1123-1136.

limits: Sample sizes are small and the samples are narrow. The arousal study rests on 24 men in its within-subject analysis, all Berkeley undergraduates, all male, answering at home on a laptop with no way for the experimenters to check what they did. Ariely and Loewenstein list that lack of control as their third limitation and the male-only sample as their fourth. Their second limitation is the one that matters most for the bias: without observing behaviour they had no way to tell whether the aroused or the non-aroused answers were the accurate ones. They say they suspect the aroused ones are, and mark it as a suspicion. Sayette and colleagues supply the missing comparison. Their cold group predicted $8.18 in session one and revised to $9.33 while craving. The hot group predicted $9.53 and revised down to $8.77, which the paper calls a trend rather than an effect. Six of their 98 participants could not understand the practice task, which used cold-water pain rather than craving, and were dropped. Loewenstein's 1996 paper contains no experiments; its evidence is drawn from other people's studies, from Styron on depression and from anecdote. The Amsterdam studies of Nordgren, van der Pligt and van Harreveld run 20 to 40 people a cell: 78 across three fatigue conditions, 148 in the follow-up, 59 in the ice-water study of which 40 reach the second stage, 69 smokers, 79 people at a cafeteria. Counting research groups rather than papers, the arousal and craving demonstrations come from Loewenstein and his co-authors, the fatigue, pain and hunger demonstrations come from one Amsterdam laboratory, and three further groups have tested versions of it: Imhoff and Schmidt on arousal, Skakoon-Sparling, Cramer and Shuper on arousal and risk in 144 and 122 participants, and Kang and Camerer on 27 people bidding to avoid eating unpleasant foods. Their average real bid was $1.92 against $1.63 hypothetical, t(49) = 9.22, p < .0001, a test run across the 50 food items rather than across the 27 bidders. With disgust and familiarity controlled the paper prints a gap of $0.20. No direct replication of the Ariely and Loewenstein procedure was located on 21 September 2026, searching Crossref, OpenAlex, Europe PMC, PubMed, Unpaywall and open web search. The nearest attempt is an unpublished Wellington master's thesis of 2022, which aroused 91 men and women with video rather than masturbation and reports a weaker effect than the original. No meta-analysis of the effect was located either, and PsycINFO was not searched.
misreadings: The arousal study is usually reported as showing that men cannot predict their aroused selves. It shows something narrower. Most of its 33 questions asked what the man found appealing or would do, not what he predicted he would do while aroused, so the non-aroused answers are current attitudes rather than forecasts. The gap is inferred from the difference between the two states. The authors say plainly that they cannot tell which set of answers is right. Retellings also place the study in a laboratory. Subjects took the laptop home, and the paper gives that as a limitation rather than a feature. The number 35 is quoted as the sample; the reported statistics rest on 24. Sayette and colleagues are cited as showing that smokers in a cold state cannot imagine craving. Their cold smokers predicted $8.18 and revised to $9.33 while craving, and the difference between the groups' actual session-two valuations was not the finding, since a preliminary test found no difference across all three conditions, F(2, 95) = 0.43, p = .65. The finding is a within-person revision. Predicting your own future state and predicting somebody else's are separate claims with separate evidence, and policy writing runs them together. The interpersonal claim rests mainly on Van Boven and Loewenstein's 47 exercisers and on the Amsterdam vignette studies, none of which compared a prediction with what the other person actually did. The 1996 paper is often cited as the source of the phrase 'hot-cold empathy gap'. It is the source of the framework and it uses different words.
